Communication-acoustics systems are increasingly embedded in larger communication systems, with more and more built-in knowledge and the ability to learn on their own. In short, communication acoustics is going cognitive. In this paper, Jens Blauert reviews the results of the EU project TWO!EARS (ICT-618075), which built a binaural model of auditory perception with cognitive components. The premise: people do not simply react to what they perceive, but to what a percept means in their current situation. Signal-processing models of hearing and vision, however refined, therefore fall short of predicting how users will experience and respond to technical systems.

The TWO!EARS model combines signal-driven (bottom-up) and hypothesis-driven (top-down) processing. It runs from ear-microphone input and peripheral auditory processing up to a “blackboard” on which expert modules interpret primitive features as auditory events, while feedback loops let knowledge about the environment steer the lower levels. The model estimates room geometry, reverberation, and the position, motion and spatial extent of sources, and delivers “where” and “what” information. Tested on a robot with auditory and visual sensors, it showed that sound localization becomes markedly faster and more precise when the commands driving head movements are taken into account along with the auditory cues. The software is open source.

The Chinese adaptation closes with likely applications, from search-and-rescue robots and smarter hearing aids to more immersive virtual reality, and with a colleague’s snapshot of Blauert at DAGA 2017.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from “Reading the World with Two Ears” by Jens Blauert, presented at ICSV 2024, the International Congress on Sound and Vibration.
